geology-geology-and-energy: Geology powers civilization: coal, oil, gas, uranium, and geothermal heat all come from the ground, and even solar and wind depend on mined metals. Geologists find these resources, map their extent, and advise on extraction. The energy transition is shifting which rocks matter — away from carbon fuels toward lithium, copper, and rare earths. Whatever the mix, the energy we use is ultimately a geological product.
geology-geologic-wonders: Geologic wonders are the planet's showpieces — places where ordinary processes created extraordinary landscapes: the basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway, the rainbow terraces of Pamukkale, the sandstone slots of Antelope Canyon, the petrified forests of Arizona. Each wonder is a geological process made visible at a dramatic scale. They draw millions of visitors, and they teach the same lessons as any outcrop: time, water, and rock, in spectacular combination.
geology-giants-causeway: The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is a sea cliff of about 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns, stepping into the Atlantic like a giant's staircase — which legend says the giant Finn MacCool built. The columns formed about 60 million years ago when lava cooled and contracted, cracking into regular polygons; the joints opened as the rock shrank. Columnar joints are common in thick basalt flows, but nowhere are they more perfect or more famous.
geology-antelope-canyon: Antelope Canyon in Arizona is a slot canyon carved by flash floods through Navajo sandstone — a narrow, twisting passage with smooth, flowing walls that glow orange, red, and purple when light enters from above. The canyon is only a few metres wide but tens of metres deep, and its curves were sculpted by water and sand over hundreds of thousands of years. It is among the most photographed places on Earth, and its beauty is pure sandstone erosion.
geology-wave-formation: The Wave, in Arizona's Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs, is a swirling sandstone formation that looks painted — undulating bands of red, orange, and white rock curving like a frozen ocean. It formed from windblown sand dunes that lithified 190 million years ago, then eroded along joints into troughs and ridges. The smooth, curved surfaces are wind-scoured and water-polished. Permits are limited to a handful of visitors a day to protect its fragile surface.
geology-white-desert: Egypt's White Desert is a stark expanse of chalk where wind carved the soft rock into surreal mushroom-shaped hoodoos and other sculptures. The chalk was once seafloor sediment, deposited when the region lay under an ancient ocean, then uplifted and eroded by desert winds for millions of years. The result is a field of white towers and arches scattered across the sand. It is geology as modern art, sculpted by the slowest artist: the wind.
geology-zabriskie-point: Zabriskie Point in Death Valley overlooks one of geology's most colourful badlands: golden, ochre, and rust ridges carved from lakebed sediment millions of years old. The badlands formed as Furnace Creek lake deposits — volcanic ash and mud — were uplifted, tilted, and then dissected by flash floods into knife-edge ridges. The colours come from iron and volcanic minerals. It is a textbook of erosion in a single sweeping view.
geology-fly-geyser: Fly Geyser in Nevada is an accidental geological wonder: a geothermal well drilled in 1964 tapped superheated water, which has been erupting and depositing mineral terraces ever since. The scalding water carries dissolved silica, which builds the growing cone and its colourful microbial mats — reds, greens, and oranges from thermophilic algae. The geyser keeps building a few centimetres a year. It shows how quickly geology can work when water and heat meet.
geology-moeraki-boulders: The Moeraki Boulders of New Zealand are giant spherical stones scattered on a beach — some over two metres across and weighing several tonnes. They are septarian concretions: calcite-cemented mud that formed around a nucleus in ancient seafloor sediment, growing outward in layers over millions of years, then exposed as the cliffs eroded. Cracks in the boulders filled with yellow calcite. They look like dinosaur eggs because, in a sense, they are geological eggs: concretions.
geology-devils-tower: Devils Tower in Wyoming is a dramatic column of igneous rock rising 265 metres above the plains — a laccolith, where magma intruded and cooled underground, then was exposed as the softer rock around it eroded. Its most striking feature is the vertical columns, some of the largest in the world. The tower's origin was long debated; Native American legends tell of a giant bear scratching the sides. The columns formed as cooling magma contracted, cracking into polygonal shafts.
geology-uluru: Uluru, the great red monolith in Australia's outback, is a giant inselberg of arkose sandstone that formed about 550 million years ago as an ancient mountain eroded and its sediment cemented into rock, then folded vertically. The rock's red colour comes from oxidized iron; its surface changes hue through the day. Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people, who have lived there for tens of thousands of years. Its sheer scale and colour make it one of the world's iconic geological sights.
geology-aztec-stone: The Twelve Apostles off Australia's Great Ocean Road are limestone stacks standing in the surf — remnants of a cliff being eroded by waves. The limestone formed from marine shells and sediment, then the sea cut caves, arches, and finally isolated stacks. The 'Twelve' number is now nine — one collapsed in 2005, watched by tourists. Each stack will eventually topple, and new arches will replace them. The Apostles are erosion in action, mid-sentence.
geology-grand-prismatic: The Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone is the largest hot spring in the United States, 90 metres across, ringed by brilliant bands of colour — deep blue centre, then green, yellow, orange, and red. The colours come from thermophilic microbes that live at different temperatures: the centre is too hot for life (blue water), while cooler edges host bacteria that tint the mat. The spring sits on the Yellowstone hotspot's heat, its water heated by magma far below.
geology-eye-of-sahara: The Eye of the Sahara, or Richat Structure, is a massive circular feature in Mauritania, 40 kilometres across, visible from space. It was once thought to be an impact crater, but it is now understood as a deeply eroded geological dome: layers of quartzite and sandstone uplifted into a dome, then eroded into concentric rings. The circular pattern forms as resistant layers stand while soft ones erode. It is one of the most photographed landmarks from orbit.
geology-pamukkale: Pamukkale in Turkey — 'cotton castle' — is a cascade of white travertine terraces built by hot springs. Calcium-rich thermal water flows down the slope, depositing calcite as it cools and loses carbon dioxide, step by step building pools and terraces that glow white against the hillside. Humans have bathed here since antiquity — the Roman city of Hierapolis sits on the terraces. The terraces grow only while the water flows; drought and tourism can dry and grey them.
geology-hanging-rock: Kjeragbolten is a five-cubic-metre boulder wedged between two cliff faces in Norway, 984 metres above a fjord — a glacial erratic stranded in a crevice when the ice retreated. Hikers queue to stand on it, suspended over the abyss, making it one of the world's most famous geology selfies. The boulder was carried and deposited by the glacier, then left balanced as the ice melted. It is gravity's most photographed balancing act.
geology-wave-rock: Wave Rock in Western Australia is a 15-metre-high granite cliff shaped like a giant breaking wave, striped by vertical bands of red, ochre, and grey. It formed from a granite inselberg's curved exfoliation surface — sheets of rock peeling away like onion layers — while mineral-laden runoff stained the surface in streaks. The 'wave' shape is an exfoliation dome exposed by erosion. It is one of Australia's most recognizable geological landmarks.
geology-crystal-cave: The Crystal Cave (Cueva de los Cristales) in Mexico holds the largest crystals on Earth — selenite gypsum beams up to 12 metres long and 55 tonnes. They grew in a cavern of superheated, mineral-saturated water for hundreds of thousands of years, at temperatures near 50°C. The cave was discovered in 2000 by miners, and it is so hot and humid that visits are limited to short, protective-gear excursions. The crystals are a glimpse of geology working at its slowest.
geology-great-blue-hole: The Great Blue Hole off Belize is a nearly perfect circular sinkhole in the ocean, 300 metres across and 124 metres deep. It formed during the ice ages, when sea level was lower: the limestone platform was exposed, groundwater dissolved a giant cavern, and its roof collapsed. When seas rose, the hole flooded. Its walls reveal limestone terraces and stalactites from the cave era, making it a favourite of divers and a record of changing sea levels.
geology-petrified-forest: The Petrified Forest in Arizona preserves 200-million-year-old trees turned to stone: logs buried by river sediment and volcanic ash, then saturated with silica-rich groundwater that replaced wood cell by cell, preserving the grain as quartz. Iron and manganese stained the fossil wood red, yellow, and purple. The petrified logs lie scattered across the desert, exposed as the rock eroded. The forest is a window into the Triassic world, and its theft is a constant park battle.
geology-geologic-wonders-list: Earth's wonders list could fill a book: the Zhangye Danxia rainbow mountains of China, Iceland's rift valley at Thingvellir, the Namib's giant dunes, Canada's Bay of Fundy tides, the Sahara's Eye of Mauritania, Bolivia's salt flats, and Hawaii's lava glow. Each is a different process at a different scale. UNESCO Geoparks preserve many of these sites for science and visitors. Wherever you stand, some local process is slowly building the next wonder.
geology-practical-geology: Practical geology is geology you can use every day: identifying the rocks in your garden wall, knowing why your basement floods, choosing stone for a patio, reading the landscape for water and slope. It includes recognizing hazard signs — cracks, tilting trees, sagging ground — and understanding what local landforms mean. Practical geology turns curiosity into competence: knowing the ground you stand on informs everything from gardening to buying a house.
geology-identifying-rocks: Identifying rocks starts with three questions: Is it igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic? Igneous rocks crystallize from melt — look for interlocking crystals; sedimentary rocks accumulate — look for layers, grains, or fossils; metamorphic rocks recrystallize under heat and pressure — look for banding or aligned minerals. Then test hardness, reaction to acid (limestone fizzes), and grain size. A hand lens, a steel nail, and dilute acid identify most rocks in the field.
geology-rock-hammer: The rock hammer is the geologist's signature tool — a pick end for prying and splitting, a flat end for chipping fresh surfaces. Used properly, it breaks rock along natural weakness to expose fresh, unweathered faces for examination. Hammer safety matters: eye protection, careful swings, and never striking hammer to hammer (steel can shatter). Many parks and protected sites forbid collecting, so the hammer is often a pointing tool these days — but it remains the symbol of the trade.
geology-field-notes-geology: Field notes are the geologist's memory: location, date, rock type, structures, and sketches, written at the outcrop while observations are fresh. A good note records measurements (strike and dip), sample numbers, and photographs, cross-referenced to a map. The discipline of field notes turns a walk into data that others can use years later. Many classic geological maps rest on notebooks kept in the field a century ago. The notebook is where geology becomes science.
geology-rock-collecting-guide: Starting a rock collection is simple: gather interesting specimens from walks, label each with where and when you found it, and identify them with a field guide or app. Build a small kit — hammer, chisel, bag, hand lens — and learn basic tests like hardness and streak. Always follow local rules: many parks prohibit collecting, and private land needs permission. A labelled collection becomes a personal geological history of everywhere you've been.
geology-home-geology: Geology is under every home: the concrete slab is crushed limestone, the tiles are fired clay or slate, the countertops are granite or quartz, and the gravel path is crushed rock. Water comes from a geological source, and drainage depends on the ground's permeability. Foundation cracks often betray soil movement, and radon seeps from uranium-bearing bedrock into basements. Understanding your home's geology explains its maintenance problems — and its sturdy bones.
geology-garden-geology: Garden geology is the ground itself: soil type decides what grows, drainage decides what drowns, and rocks from the subsoil or glacial deposits pepper the beds. Lime-loving plants need alkaline soil from limestone country; acid lovers need the peaty, sandy ground of granite or sandstone regions. Digging reveals your local geology — clay from shale, sand from sandstone, pebbles from glacial gravel. Gardeners who know their soil's origin garden with the ground instead of against it.
geology-rock-gardens: Rock gardens display geology as much as plants: the rocks — often local stone — provide structure, drainage, and a microclimate for alpine plants, and they echo the natural scree and cliff communities of mountain regions. A well-built rock garden uses layers and cracks like a natural outcrop, giving plants niches. The stones also tell a story: limestone brings alkaline drainage, granite brings acidity, and slate splits into steps. Rock gardens are miniature landscapes built on real geological principles.
geology-stone-walls: Dry-stone walls are ancient engineering that reads the local geology: every wall is built of the rock at hand — limestone, sandstone, granite, or slate — laid by skilled hands without mortar. The builders chose flat, strong stones and stacked them to shed water and resist frost heave. Old walls reveal the area's rock types and field history, and some are centuries old, still standing. A dry-stone wall is geology sorted, shaped, and set by human hands.
geology-pebbles: A pebble is a geological story in your pocket: it was broken from bedrock, rounded by rivers or waves, and carried — perhaps for hundreds of kilometres — before being dropped. Its shape tells how far it travelled: sharp means fresh, rounded means long journey. Its composition tells its source: quartz from veins, flint from chalk, granite from mountains. Geologists read pebble beaches and gravels as archives of a region's erosion history.
geology-beach-combing-geology: Beachcombing for rocks turns a walk into a field trip: each pebble and boulder on the beach was transported from somewhere and sorted by the waves. Rock beaches sort by density and size — the heavy, resistant rocks like flint and quartz stay; the soft ones grind to sand. Agates, fossils, and sea glass hide among the cobbles. Reading a beach's mix of rocks reveals what lies inland and offshore, carried down rivers and along the coast by the sea.
geology-gem-hunting: Gem hunting combines prospecting with patience: gems concentrate where geology puts them — pegmatite veins for quartz and tourmaline, gravel beds for agate and jasper, volcanic rocks for opal, and metamorphic zones for garnet. Good hunting grounds include river gravels, tailings from old mines, and exposed volcanic or pegmatite outcrops. Tools are simple: hammer, chisel, sieve, and a bucket of water. Finding a gem in its natural setting is one of geology's purest thrills.
geology-rock-tumbling: Rock tumbling turns rough stones into gems: a barrel of rocks, grit, and water rotates for weeks, progressively finer grit polishing the stones as they tumble against each other — the same process that rounds river pebbles, accelerated. Agates, jasper, and quartz tumble well; soft rocks crumble. The hobby teaches mineral hardness and fracture — the same properties geologists use to identify rocks. A tumbled stone is a river-polished pebble made by machine.
geology-fossil-hunting-guide: Beginner fossil hunting starts with the right places: sedimentary rocks — limestone, shale, sandstone — especially along riverbanks, quarries, road cuts, and sea cliffs. Look for layered exposures, and search for shells, ripple marks, or bones; split shale along its layers. Bring a hammer, chisel, and bag, and never collect from parks without permission. The best finds are often small and humble — but every fossil is a life that outlasted its world.
geology-meteorite-testing: Testing a suspected meteorite starts with clues: most meteorites are magnetic (they contain iron), denser than ordinary rocks, and show a dark fusion crust where they melted entering the atmosphere. A streak test helps — meteorites rarely leave a coloured streak. Regmaglypts, thumbprint-like depressions, and a fresh metal flash on a cut surface are strong signs. Only a laboratory analysis can confirm a meteorite, but field tests separate likely candidates from ordinary iron-rich rocks.
geology-stone-knapping: Stone knapping is the ancient craft of shaping rock by controlled fracture — striking flint, chert, or obsidian to produce sharp flakes and blades. It demands understanding the rock's fracture properties: conchoidal fracture, like glass, lets skilled knappers control the break. Knapping produced tools for three million years and still teaches modern archaeologists and geologists about raw material choice and human skill. A flint flake is the oldest manufactured technology.
geology-crystal-growing: Growing crystals at home is geology in miniature: dissolve salt, sugar, or alum in hot water, suspend a seed crystal, and watch the solution cool and evaporate, depositing material layer by layer — the same process that grows minerals in nature, but in days instead of millennia. Crystal shape follows chemistry: salt cubes, alum octahedra, sugar needles. The hobby teaches saturation, nucleation, and crystal habit — the same physics that builds gems deep underground.
geology-geology-books: Geology is wonderfully readable: classics like John McPhee's Basin and Range, Simon Winchester's Krakatoa and The Map That Changed the World, and Richard Fortey's Earth tell the science as story. Field guides by region teach identification, and textbooks from Marshak to Tarbuck lay out the whole discipline. Books carry geology's greatest asset — deep time — into the mind at reading pace. For beginners, one good field guide and one good history are the perfect start.
geology-geology-apps: Geology apps put a field kit in your pocket: Rockd identifies rocks and maps local geology from your location, StraboSpot supports field data collection, and the USGS Earthquakes app streams quake data live. Mineral and fossil identification apps use photos and properties; satellite and map apps like Google Earth show regional structure from orbit. While apps can't replace a hammer and hand lens, they turn any walk into a geological survey — and they're free.
geology-practical-geology-careers: Practical geology is itself a career path: geotechnical technicians test soils for construction, hydrogeologists work water projects, mineral exploration crews find ores, and environmental geologists clean contaminated sites. Many roles need only a bachelor's degree plus field training, and they pay well and travel widely. Practical geology's appeal is direct: you use science to solve real, ground-level problems every day — from a sinking foundation to a vanishing aquifer.
geology-grand-canyon-geology-2: The Grand Canyon is deep time carved into rock: its walls stack nearly two billion years of history, from the ancient schist at the bottom to the Kaibab Limestone at the rim. The Colorado River began cutting about six million years ago as the plateau rose, and it still deepens the gorge. Each formation records a different world — desert dunes, shallow seas, coastal swamps. Walking rim to rim is walking a billion years, one layer at a time.
geology-great-barrier-reef-geology-2: The Great Barrier Reef is a geological formation built by living organisms: coral polyps extract calcium carbonate from seawater and cement it into limestone, building a structure visible from space. The modern reef grew on Pleistocene foundations as seas rose over the past 20,000 years, and it rests on Australia's ancient continental shelf. Its 2,900 reefs are a living sediment factory — and a sensitive recorder of ocean temperature and chemistry.
geology-marble-arch: The Marble Arch Caves in Northern Ireland wind through 340-million-year-old limestone, where rivers carved passages along bedding planes and joints, dissolving the rock into caves, chambers, and waterfalls. Named for a natural arch where the river flows beneath rock, the cave system is one of Europe's finest show caves. The water still dissolves the limestone, slowly enlarging the passages. Marble Arch is karst geology at its most beautiful — and most visitable.
geology-petrified-forest-2: Arizona's Petrified Forest preserves a Triassic world: 200-million-year-old logs buried in river sediment and ash, then saturated with silica that crystallized as quartz inside the wood, cell by cell. The result is stone logs that preserve the grain, rings, and even worm holes of the originals, stained red and purple by iron. Erosion now scatters the petrified logs across the desert floor. The forest is a fossil ecosystem, preserved in mineral detail.
geology-giants-causeway-2: The Giant's Causeway's 40,000 hexagonal columns formed when Paleocene lava cooled and contracted, cracking into regular polygons — mostly hexagons because that shape packs most efficiently. The columns rise like organ pipes from the sea, each up to 12 metres tall, and the formation continues underwater and inland. Similar columnar joints appear in basalt flows worldwide, but the Causeway's size and perfection make it the type example. It is Northern Ireland's geological icon.
geology-wave-rock-2: Wave Rock's 15-metre wave-shaped cliff is an exfoliation dome: as erosion removed overlying rock, the granite expanded and shed curved sheets, creating the smooth overhanging face. Rainwater runoff stained the surface in vertical stripes of red and ochre, and weathered the rock into the wave form. It has been shaped over millions of years and continues to peel. Wave Rock shows that even the hardest rock can bend — slowly — under the right conditions.
geology-salar-de-uyuni-2: The Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat, a 10,000-square-kilometre crust of salt covering a prehistoric lake bed at 3,650 metres altitude. When the lake evaporated, it left salt up to 10 metres thick over layers of lake sediment and brine. The flat is so perfectly level that satellites use it for calibration, and its lithium-rich brine makes it a global resource. In the wet season, a film of water turns it into a mirror of the sky.
geology-great-blue-hole-2: The Great Blue Hole is a circular collapse sinkhole in Belize's Lighthouse Reef — 300 metres across, 124 metres deep, with walls that drop sheer into dark blue water. It formed during the last ice age when sea level fell, exposing the limestone platform; groundwater dissolved a cave system, and its roof later collapsed. Stalactites still hang at depth from the flooded cave. Divers descend past the limestone ledges — a journey into a drowned cave's history.
geology-mid-atlantic-ridge: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth — a 16,000-kilometre underwater chain where the seafloor spreads apart, creating new oceanic crust. Iceland is its only part that rises above the sea, where visitors can literally stand on the rift between two tectonic plates. The ridge is the source of the magnetic stripe pattern that proved seafloor spreading, and it hosts hydrothermal vents and their unique ecosystems. It is Earth's great wound, still healing with new rock.
geology-rock-of-gibraltar: The Rock of Gibraltar is a monolithic limestone promontory guarding the Mediterranean's western gateway — a Jurassic limestone block, part of the Betic mountain belt, uplifted as Africa and Europe collided. Its famous caves, including St. Michael's Cave, are karst features carved by groundwater. The Rock's position made it a fortress for over a thousand years. Geologically, it is a mountain of ancient seafloor standing sentinel over the strait.
geology-aurora-and-rocks: The aurora borealis leaves no rock record, but its cause — the solar wind and Earth's magnetic field — shaped the geology around it. The magnetic field that funnels auroras to the poles is generated in Earth's liquid outer core, and its reversals are frozen into the rocks as magnetic stripes. Ancient auroral activity accompanied stronger solar storms, which may have driven early atmospheric chemistry. The lights in the sky and the stripes in the seafloor share an origin: Earth's magnetic dynamo.
geology-moonstone: Moonstone is a feldspar mineral that glows with a floating blue-white sheen — adularescence — caused by light scattering between microscopic crystal layers. It forms in pegmatites and has been treasured for millennia: Romans linked it to the Moon, Indians called it the 'dream stone', and Art Nouveau jewellers made it iconic. Its sheen is pure physics — the same light play that gives opal and labradorite their glow. Moonstone is a mineral that looks like captured moonlight.
geology-amber-and-time: Amber is fossilized tree resin, not stone — sticky sap that hardened and polymerized over millions of years, sometimes trapping insects, leaves, and even feathers in perfect detail. Most amber dates from the Cretaceous and Eocene, when resin-producing forests were widespread; Baltic amber, up to 50 million years old, has been traded for thousands of years. Amber preserves a window into ancient forests, and its inclusions have even yielded fragments of dinosaur-era DNA. It is time in a bottle.
geology-oolitic-limestone: Oolitic limestone is built of ooids — tiny, spherical calcium carbonate grains that formed as seawater agitated and coated sediment grains with concentric layers, like microscopic pearls. The ooids accumulated in warm, shallow, wave-stirred seas, then cemented into stone. Jurassic oolitic limestone built much of Bath and Oxford in England, prized as building stone. The 'egg stone' shows how sediment can grow, not just settle — a deposit built grain by grain in rolling water.
geology-flint-knapping: Flint, a hard form of silica found in chalk, was the first industrial material: knappable to razor edges, fire-striking, and widely traded for hundreds of thousands of years. Flint axes, arrowheads, and blades shaped human history, and flint's conchoidal fracture made it ideal for controlled knapping. Its use spanned the Stone Age into the gunflint era of the 1800s. Flint is geology that changed the course of technology — a stone that made civilization possible.
geology-black-smokers: Black smokers are hydrothermal vents on the mid-ocean ridges: superheated, mineral-rich water blasts from the seafloor and precipitates black clouds of metal sulphides, building chimneys that can grow tens of metres tall. The vents host ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis — bacteria converting vent chemicals into food, supporting tube worms, shrimp, and crabs. They were discovered in 1977 and are now studied as models for the origin of life on Earth and beyond. Black smokers are geology's most alien neighbourhood.
geology-seafloor-spreading-evidence: Seafloor spreading was proven by three lines of evidence: magnetic stripes — parallel bands of normal and reversed polarity frozen in the basalt, symmetric about the ridges; age progression — seafloor grows older away from ridges; and drilling — sediment thickness and radiometric dates matching the spreading prediction. Harry Hess proposed the mechanism in 1960; Vine and Matthews decoded the stripes in 1963. Within a decade, the seafloor's quiet record had transformed geology into plate tectonics.
geology-lithified-sand-dunes: Lithified sand dunes are fossilized deserts: giant cross-bedded sandstones like the Navajo and Coconino formations record ancient dune fields that once covered parts of the American Southwest. The sweeping diagonal bedding preserved in the rock is a cross-section of dune migration, grain layer by grain layer. These petrified dunes, some 200 million years old, tell of a time when the region was a vast Sahara. Climbing the Vermilion Cliffs is walking across a drowned desert.
geology-glacial-striations: Glacial striations are scratches on bedrock left by rocks dragged beneath moving ice — the signature of glaciers long gone. The scratches align with ice flow, so geologists use them to map the direction ancient ice moved. Erratics — boulders carried far from their source — confirm the journey. Striated pavements from the last ice age, polished and grooved, are scattered across Canada, Scandinavia, and the northern United States. They are the footprints of vanished ice sheets.
geology-batholith: A batholith is a vast body of granite formed when a giant plume of magma cooled deep underground — the 'frozen magma sea' beneath mountain ranges. The Sierra Nevada batholith, one of the world's largest, spans 600 kilometres of California and fed the range's volcanic past. Erosion has exposed the granite core, forming the famous domes of Yosemite. Batholiths record the deep roots of volcanic arcs, and their exposure tells the story of mountain building and unroofing.
